newsitem.title: USA: Ailing social spending projects may derail Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Ailing social spending projects may derail Clinton.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent

President Bill Clinton wants to build a bridge to the 21st century but it may end up riddled with potholes if nothing is done to patch up social spending programmes that threaten to bankrupt the government.

Analysts said newly re-elected Clinton needs to work with the Republican-led Congress to reform the Medicaid, Medicare and Social Security programmes before their costs balloon in the next century as the baby-boom generation reaches retirement.
"For reform to be humane we must act now, not when the crisis is upon us, for then the choices will be truly draconian," former Commerce Secretary Pete Peterson said.

Simply balancing the budget by 2002, as both Democrat Clinton and Republican lawmakers have pledged to do, will not be enough, analysts said. The government must rein in spending on entitlement programmes -- Medicare and Medicaid health care for the elderly and poor and the Social Security pension system -- to put its long-term finances on a sound footing.
"Trying to balance the budget without reforming entitlements is like trying to clean out the garage without removing the Winnebago," Peterson said. "It cannot be done."
The Congressional Budget Office has warned that the three entitlement programmes will place "unprecedented pressure" on federal spending starting in 2010.

"Indeed, by the middle of the next century, they threaten to drive the federal debt to levels that the economy could not possibly sustain," the non-partisan office, which advises Congress on budget matters, said in a recent report.
For Medicare, the crunch will come much sooner. The $128 billion trust fund that pays medical bills for the elderly lost $4.2 billion last year and is widely expected to go bankrupt in 2001.

Clinton has proposed cutting back the growth of Medicare spending by $124 billion over the next six years, mainly by reducing payments to hospitals and doctors. Republican lawmakers have advocated $168 billion in savings.
Given the hammering that the Republicans took during the election campaign on the issue, analysts said Clinton will have to take the initiative in working out a compromise.

"It's going to take the president to lead in this area," said Steve Bell, who heads his own consulting company in Washington. That will be be the test of whether Clinton can work with the new Congress next year, Bell added.
But even if an agreement can be hammered out, that would only extend the life of the Medicare programme for about 10 years. Significant reforms would be needed for the long run.
"The 10-year fix is not a permanent one," acknowledged White House chief economist Joseph Stiglitz.

Clinton has called for a joint effort between Democrats and Republicans -- perhaps a high-powered bilateral commission -- to address longer-term problems facing Medicare, Social Security and Medicaid, the health care programme for the poor.
Some analysts have even suggested that Clinton appoint the man he beat for the presidency, former Republican Sen. Bob Dole, as head of the commission.

The administration already has a bipartisan panel in place to advise it on Social Security that is expected to publish its recommendations next month. But the 13-member group remains split over what steps to take to ensure the continued viability of the programme, although all agree on investing a portion of the $400 billion of the Social Security taxes collected each year in the stock market.

The proceeds of the 12.4 percent Social Security payroll tax, which is borne by both employers and employees, are currently invested in Treasury bonds, which over time yield less of a return than money put in the stock market.
Other measures that have been discussed by the panel include increasing the eligibility age for Social Security payments and reducing benefits for higher-income workers.
Analysts estimate that Social Security will face an annual cash deficit of more than $750 billion by 2030 if nothing is done to reform the system.
